questions.q: In Task 1, `Y @ Y.conj().T` produces the identity matrix for Pauli-Y. What specific complex multiplication on the diagonal makes this work out to exactly 1?
options: (-j)(j) = -j^2 = 1 on one diagonal entry, and (j)(-j) = -j^2 = 1 on the other, since j^2 = -1
The off-diagonal zeros are multiplied together to produce 1 directly
NumPy automatically rounds any nonzero diagonal entry up to 1
Y's entries are all real numbers, so no complex multiplication is actually involved
questions.explain: Y's nonzero entries are -j and j. Multiplying Y by its conjugate transpose pairs (-j) with (j) on the diagonal: (-j)(j) = -j^2 = -(-1) = 1, landing exactly on the identity matrix.

questions.q: Task 2 shows `is_unitary(S)` returns True while `is_hermitian(S)` returns False for the S-gate. What in S's structure causes this specific combination of results?
options: S @ S.conj().T still produces the identity matrix (since (j)(-j)=1), but S itself has j in its corner while S.conj().T has -j there, so S != S.conj().T
S is actually equal to the identity matrix, which is both unitary and Hermitian trivially
is_hermitian always returns False for any matrix containing a complex number
The two functions check the exact same condition, so they should always agree, and this result indicates a bug
questions.explain: S@S.conj().T = I confirms unitarity regardless of the sign of the imaginary entry, since (j)(-j)=1 either way. But S itself and S.conj().T differ in the sign of that imaginary entry (j vs -j), so they are not equal, meaning S fails the Hermitian check.

questions.q: For the Hermitian matrix A = [[2, 1+1j], [1-1j, 3]], the lesson computes trace=5 and det=4, then solves lambda^2 - 5*lambda + 4 = 0 to get eigenvalues 1 and 4. Why does the off-diagonal product (1+1j)(1-1j) come out as a real number (2), making this determinant calculation real-valued?
options: (1+1j)(1-1j) is a product of a complex number and its own conjugate, which always equals a real number -- specifically |1+1j|^2 = 1^2+1^2 = 2
It is a coincidence specific to this matrix and would not happen for any other Hermitian matrix
NumPy rounds the imaginary part to zero automatically whenever a determinant is computed
The off-diagonal entries were chosen incorrectly and should have produced an imaginary determinant
questions.explain: Because A is Hermitian, its off-diagonal entries are complex conjugates of each other (1+1j and 1-1j). Multiplying a complex number by its own conjugate always gives a real result (the squared modulus), which is exactly why a Hermitian matrix's determinant -- and its eigenvalues -- always come out real.

questions.q: `np.linalg.eigvals(A)` returns `[1.+0.j, 4.+0.j]` while `np.linalg.eigvalsh(A)` returns `[1., 4.]` for the same Hermitian matrix A. Why do the two functions return different-looking output for identical eigenvalues?
options: eigvals is general-purpose and always returns complex dtype since it can't assume the imaginary part is exactly zero; eigvalsh assumes the matrix is Hermitian and returns real dtype directly
eigvals and eigvalsh actually compute different, unrelated quantities that happen to coincide here
eigvalsh is less accurate than eigvals and rounds away a real imaginary component
The difference is a display bug in NumPy with no underlying cause
questions.explain: eigvals works on any square matrix and so must carry a complex dtype in its result array (even when the imaginary parts are zero), while eigvalsh is specialized for Hermitian input and both runs faster and guarantees a real-dtype result, since Hermitian matrices are mathematically guaranteed to have real eigenvalues.

questions.q: The lab states that 'every Hermitian matrix has entirely real eigenvalues, regardless of how many complex entries it contains off the diagonal.' Why does this matter physically for how quantum mechanics uses Hermitian matrices?
options: A measurement outcome (like energy or spin) must be a real number, and representing observables as Hermitian matrices guarantees that by construction, no matter how complex the matrix's entries look
It matters only mathematically and has no connection to anything measurable in a real experiment
It guarantees the matrix is also unitary, so gates and observables are interchangeable
It means Hermitian matrices can never contain the imaginary unit j anywhere in their entries
questions.explain: Physical measurement outcomes must be real numbers. Because Hermitian matrices are mathematically guaranteed to have real eigenvalues, using them to represent observables (energy, spin, etc.) guarantees that any predicted measurement outcome will be real -- exactly the property physics needs, built into the linear algebra.
